claim: Most amino acids can be encoded by several synonymous codons, which are used at unequal frequencies.
source: Most amino acids can be encoded by several synonymous codons, which are used at unequal frequencies.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the genetic code and codon usage patterns.

claim: Different codons are decoded at different rates in the A-site.
source: Different codons are decoded at different rates in the A-site.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental ribosome profiling data and RRT analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: In general, frequent codons are decoded more quickly than rare codons.
source: In general, frequent codons are decoded more quickly than rare codons, and AT-rich codons are decoded more quickly than GC-rich codons.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 5A and the RRT measurements in Table 2.

claim: AT-rich codons are decoded more quickly than GC-rich codons.
source: In general, frequent codons are decoded more quickly than rare codons, and AT-rich codons are decoded more quickly than GC-rich codons.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 5B comparing GC content with RRT values.

claim: At the P-site, proline is slow in forming peptide bonds.
source: At the P-site, proline is slow in forming peptide bonds.
evidence: This is supported by the RRT analysis showing high values for proline codons at position 5 (P-site) as shown in Figure 4D and Table 2.

claim: Different synonymous codons have been debated for three decades regarding the reasons for biased codon usage.
source: Different synonymous codons are used in genes at very different frequencies, and the reasons for this biased codon usage have been debated for three decades (Fitch, 1976; Hasegawa et al., 1979; Miyata et al., 1979; Bennetzen and Hall, 1982; Lipman and Wilbur, 1983; Sharp and Li, 1986; Bulmer, 1987; Drummond and Wilke, 2008) (reviewed by Plotkin and Kudla (2011); Forster (2012); Novoa and Ribas de Pouplana (2012)).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to historical literature on codon usage bias.

claim: It has been suggested that frequently-used codons are translated more rapidly than rarely-used codons, perhaps because tRNAs for the frequent codons are relatively highly expressed.
source: In particular, it has been suggested that the frequently-used codons are translated more rapidly than rarely-used codons, perhaps because tRNAs for the frequent codons are relatively highly expressed (Plotkin and Kudla, 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature cited.

claim: There is little or no direct in vivo evidence as to whether the more common codons are indeed translated more rapidly than the rarer codons.
source: There is little or no direct in vivo evidence as to whether the more common codons are indeed translated more rapidly than the rarer codons.
evidence: This statement characterizes the state of the field prior to this study.

claim: Translation is typically limited by initiation, not elongation.
source: Even if they are, the fact that translation is typically limited by initiation, not elongation, leaves the effectiveness of codon optimization a puzzle (Plotkin and Kudla, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited literature.

claim: Ribosome profiling allows the observation of positions of ribosomes on translating cellular mRNAs.
source: Ribosome profiling (Ingolia et al., 2009) allows the observation of positions of ribosomes on translating cellular mRNAs.
evidence: This describes the established ribosome profiling method from the cited literature.

claim: A translating ribosome protects a region of mRNA from nuclease digestion, generating a 30 base 'footprint'.
source: The basis of the method is that a translating ribosome protects a region of mRNA from nuclease digestion, generating a 30 base 'footprint'.
evidence: This describes the technical basis of ribosome profiling.

claim: The ribosome footprint is roughly centered on the A-site of the ribosome.
source: The footprint is roughly centered on the A-site of the ribosome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ribosome profiling methodology.

claim: If some particular codon in the A-site were translated slowly, then the ribosome would dwell at this position, and so footprints generated from ribosomes at this position would be relatively common.
source: If some particular codon in the A-site were translated slowly, then the ribosome would dwell at this position, and so footprints generated from ribosomes at this position would be relatively common.
evidence: This is a logical inference about how ribosome profiling data relates to translation kinetics.

claim: There is dramatic variation in the number of footprints generated at different positions along any particular mRNA.
source: Experimentally, there is dramatic variation in the number of footprints generated at different positions along any particular mRNA (Ingolia et al., 2011) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature and Figure 1 showing footprint profiles.

claim: Large peaks and valleys in ribosome footprint profiles do not correlate with particular codons.
source: However, these large peaks and valleys do not correlate with particular codons (Ingolia et al., 2011; Charneski and Hurst, 2013).
evidence: This is based on findings from cited literature.

claim: There is evidence that prolines, or a poly-basic amino acid stretch, contribute to a slowing of the ribosome and a peak of ribosome footprints.
source: It is still unclear what features of the mRNA cause the peaks and valleys, though there is evidence that prolines, or a poly-basic amino acid stretch, contribute to a slowing of the ribosome and a peak of ribosome footprints (Ingolia et al., 2011; Brandman et al., 2012; Charneski and Hurst, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Qian et al. (2012) and Charneski and Hurst (2013) found no effect of different synonymous codons on translation rate using yeast ribosome profiling data.
source: This question was investigated by Qian et al. (2012) and Charneski and Hurst (2013) using the yeast ribosome profiling data of Ingolia et al. (2009). Neither group found any effect of different synonymous codons on translation rate—that is, perhaps surprisingly, each codon, rare or common, appeared to be translated at the same rate (Qian et al., 2012; Charneski and Hurst, 2013).
evidence: This summarizes findings from cited previous studies.

claim: The current study generated four yeast ribosome profiling datasets by optimized methods, including flash-freezing of growing cells before the addition of cycloheximide.
source: First, we have generated four yeast ribosome profiling datasets by optimized methods, including the flash-freezing of growing cells before the addition of cycloheximide ('Materials and methods'); Ingolia et al. added cycloheximide before harvesting cells.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the current study.

claim: The current study developed a novel method of analysis designed with the knowledge that codon decoding rates could account for only a small portion of the variation in ribosome footprints across an mRNA.
source: Second, we have developed a novel method of analysis, designed with the knowledge that, at best, codon decoding rates could account for only a small portion of the variation in ribosome footprints across an mRNA ('Materials and methods').
evidence: This describes the analytical approach developed in the study.

claim: The combination of optimized data and novel analysis reveals that different codons are decoded at different rates.
source: The combination of optimized data and novel analysis reveals that different codons are decoded at different rates.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data and analysis.

claim: Previous analysis of ribosome profiling data overweighted highly expressed genes, which account for a large fraction of total reads.
source: However, this analysis in its simplest form would overweight the highly expressed genes, which account for a large fraction of total reads—that is, a relatively small number of highly expressed genes would dominate the analysis.
evidence: This is a logical inference about potential biases in previous analytical approaches.

claim: The study analyzed many selected regions (windows) where the effects of codon usage are particularly easy to assay.
source: Instead, we have opted for a simpler approach. We independently analyze many selected regions (windows) where the effects of codon usage are particularly easy to assay.
evidence: This describes the analytical strategy used in the study.

claim: For each codon, the study identified all translated regions in the genome where a particular codon occurs uniquely within a window of 10 codons upstream and 10 codons downstream.
source: For each codon, we identify all translated regions in the genome where a particular codon (say CTC) occurs uniquely within a window of 10 codons upstream and 10 codons downstream—that is, a window 19-codons wide, with the codon of interest occurring exactly once at position 10 of the 19-position window.
evidence: This describes the specific analytical method used.

claim: For the four datasets, there was an average of 408, 1586, 1749, or 2868 qualifying windows per codon, respectively.
source: For our four datasets discussed below, there was an average of 408, 1586, 1749, or 2868 qualifying windows per codon, respectively (more windows for the abundant codons, fewer for the rare codons).
evidence: This provides quantitative information about the data analyzed.

claim: In the absence of any codon preference of the ribosome, there should be a uniform distribution of footprints across the ten positions.
source: In the absence of any codon preference of the ribosome, there should be a uniform distribution of footprints across the ten positions.
evidence: This is a logical expectation based on the null hypothesis.

claim: The Ribosome Residence Time (RRT) is a statistic that compares the average relative frequency for a codon at a particular position to the baseline frequency (0.1).
source: The relative frequency averaged over all windows is a number between 0 and 1, and we compare this to the baseline frequency (0.1) (total footprints over 10 positions) to compute a final statistic, which we call the Ribosome Residence Time, or RRT.
evidence: This defines the RRT metric developed in the study.

claim: An RRT of 1 means that the ribosome spends the average amount of time at the given codon at the given position.
source: For instance, if the average relative frequency for a codon at a particular position is 0.1, then the RRT is 1, and we interpret this to mean that the ribosome spends the average amount of time at the given codon at the given position.
evidence: This explains the interpretation of the RRT metric.

claim: An RRT of two suggests that the ribosome spends twice as long as average at the given codon.
source: An RRT of two suggests that the ribosome spends twice as long as average at the given codon.
evidence: This explains the interpretation of the RRT metric.

claim: For a simulated negative control, all codons at all positions show an RRT of about 1, indicating no signal.
source: For a simulated negative control, we assigned real footprint data from our SC-lys dataset to random codons and did RRT analysis. As expected, all codons at all positions show an RRT of about 1, that is, no signal (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the simulated control experiment shown in Figure 2A.

claim: For a simulated positive control with biased reads for codon AAA at position 6, RRT analysis shows a peak for AAA at position 6.
source: For a simulated positive control, we generated a simulated data set of 2 million 10-codon reads over coding genes, but we biased these simulated reads to give more reads for the codon AAA at position 6 of the footprint. As expected, RRT analysis shows a peak for AAA at position 6 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the simulated control experiment shown in Figure 2B.

claim: RRT analysis of naked RNA fragments (real data negative control) shows no peaks in positions 2 through 9.
source: For a real-data negative control, we pooled the control mRNA-seq data for 30 bp fragments from our four experiments ('Materials and methods') and analyzed these mRNA fragments. Since this RNA came from a total naked RNA preparation, there were no ribosomes and no ribosome footprints, so there should not be any signal from translation, even though we are analyzing real 30 bp RNA fragments. Indeed, RRT analysis shows no peaks in positions 2 through 9 of these fragments (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the control experiment shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There are modest deviations from 1 at the termini (positions 1 and 10) in the naked RNA control, attributed to base-specificity for enzymatic reactions used to generate the fragment library.
source: However, there are modest deviations from 1 at the termini, positions 1 and 10. We attribute these to some base-specificity for the enzymatic reactions used to generate the fragment library (Lamm et al., 2011; Jackson et al., 2014; Raabe et al., 2014).
evidence: This interpretation is supported by citations to literature on enzymatic biases.

claim: In E. coli starved for serine, all six serine codons have high RRT values at position 8.
source: For a real data positive control experiment, we used the Escherichia coli data generated by Li et al., who starved E. coli for serine, and did ribosome profiling (Li et al., 2012). Because of the starvation for serine, there is an expectation that all six serine codons should be decoded slowly and so should have high RRT values. This proved to be the case (Figure 2D). The six serine codons had 6 of the 7 highest RRT values at position 8 (Figure 2D, Table 1), which presumably represents the A-site in this experiment.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of published E. coli data shown in Figure 2D and Table 1.

claim: In E. coli ribosomes, the phase of the footprint (i.e., the position of the A-site in the footprint) is different from its phase with regard to yeast ribosomes.
source: Note that because these are E. coli ribosomes, the phase of the footprint (i.e., the position of the A-site in the footprint) is different from its phase with regard to yeast ribosomes (see below).
evidence: This is inferred from the different peak positions observed in E. coli vs yeast data.

claim: In a large majority of cases, a codon has its highest or lowest footprint abundance when the codon is in position 6.
source: Figure 4 shows data for all 61 sense codons from one of four experiments, the 'SC-lys' experiment. In a large majority of cases, a codon has its highest or lowest footprint abundance when the codon is in position 6.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Position 6 is interpreted to be the A-site of the ribosome.
source: We interpret this to mean that the codon affects the rate of ribosome movement when the codon is in position 6, which we believe to be the A-site of the ribosome (see below for further support for this assignment).
evidence: This interpretation is based on the pattern of RRT peaks and is supported by control experiments.

claim: Footprint frequencies differ from the average in a specific way at position 5.
source: Footprint frequencies also differ from the average in a specific way at positions 5 (Figure 4D) (see below) and 1 and 10, the two ends of the footprint.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D for proline codons.

claim: Variation at positions 1 and 10 is attributed to base-specificity for the enzymatic reactions involved in generating and analyzing ribosome footprints.
source: We attribute variation at positions 1 and 10 to some base-specificity for the enzymatic reactions involved in generating and analyzing ribosome footprints (Lamm et al., 2011; Jackson et al., 2014; Raabe et al., 2014); the same variations are seen in reactions with naked RNA fragments.
evidence: This interpretation is supported by citations and by the observation of similar patterns in naked RNA controls.

claim: There is a good correlation (r = –0.52) between the deduced rate of ribosome movement for each codon and the frequency of codon usage.
source: Figure 5A shows the deduced rate of ribosome movement for each codon, plotted against the frequency of codon usage. There is a good correlation (r = –0.52); that is, the ribosome moves faster over the more common codons.
evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There is a correlation between RRT and the AT-richness of the codon, with AT-rich codons decoded somewhat faster than average and GC-rich codons decoded more slowly.
source: There is also a correlation, albeit weaker, with the AT-richness of the codon. AT-rich codons are decoded somewhat faster than average, while GC-rich codons are decoded more slowly (Figure 5B).
evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The mean RRT of codons with 3 or 2 GC residues was 1.23, while the mean RRT of codons with 1 or 0 GC residues was 1.01, a statistically significant difference (p < 0.003).
source: The mean RRT of codons with 3 or 2 GC residues was 1.23, while the mean RRT of codons with 1 or 0 GC residues was 1.01, a statistically significant difference (p < 0.003 by a two-tailed t test).
evidence: This statistical comparison is provided with a p-value.

claim: The slowest codon is the rare Leu codon CTC with an RRT of about 1.9.
source: Table 2 shows the Ribosome Residence Time at position 6 for each of the 61 sense codons. The slowest codon is the rare Leu codon CTC. Relatively, the ribosome spends about 1.9 times as long with a CTC codon in the A site as it does at the average codon.
evidence: This is shown in Table 2.

claim: The fastest codon is the relatively abundant Thr codon ACC with an RRT of 0.70.
source: The fastest codon is the relatively abundant Thr codon ACC (Figure 4C, Table 2), where it spends 0.70 times as long as average (i.e., about 35 milliseconds).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C and Table 2.

claim: If the yeast ribosome spends 50 milliseconds on an average codon in the A-site, then it spends about 95 milliseconds on CTC codons.
source: If the yeast ribosome spends 50 milliseconds (Futcher et al., 1999) on an average codon in the A-site, then the RRT suggests it spends about 95 milliseconds on CTC codons.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the RRT value and a cited estimate of average codon dwell time.

claim: All four Pro codons are high at position 5: CCT, CCA, and CCC are the three slowest codons at position 5, while CCG is 6th.
source: There are also peaks at position 5 (Figure 4A,D), which we interpret as the ribosome's P-site, where the peptide bond is formed. All four Pro codons are high at position 5: CCT, CCA, and CCC are the three slowest codons at position 5, while CCG is 6th (Figure 4D, Table 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D and Table 2.

claim: Proline is a unique amino acid in having a secondary rather than a primary amino group, and so it is less reactive in peptide bond formation.
source: Proline is a unique amino acid in having a secondary rather than a primary amino group, and so it is less reactive in peptide bond formation.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about proline structure.

claim: Proline forms peptide bonds slowly.
source: Proline forms peptide bonds slowly (Muto and Ito, 2008; Wohlgemuth et al., 2008; Pavlov et al., 2009; Johansson et al., 2011), and proline has been associated with slow translation in footprinting experiments (Ingolia et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The result that the ribosome slows with proline at position 5 is consistent with proline's slow peptide bond formation and tends to confirm the assignment of position 5 to the P-site and position 6 to the A-site.
source: Our result that the ribosome slows with proline at position 5 is consistent with this and tends to confirm our assignment of position 5 to the P-site and, therefore, position 6 to the A-site.
evidence: This is an inference based on the consistency of the data with known biochemistry.

claim: A few other residues also seem slightly slow at position 5 (e.g., Asn, Gly), possibly due to low reactivity in peptide bond formation.
source: A few other residues also seem slightly slow at position 5 (e.g., Asn, Gly, see Table 2 and Supplementary file 1), possibly due to low reactivity in peptide bond formation (Johansson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on data in Table 2 and a cited reference about peptide bond formation kinetics.

claim: All four proline codons also have high RRTs at position 6, the A-site.
source: All four proline codons also have high RRTs at position 6, the A-site (Figure 4D, Table 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D and Table 2.

claim: The dipeptide ProPro is translated very slowly.
source: The dipeptide ProPro is translated very slowly (Doerfel et al., 2013; Gutierrez et al., 2013; Peil et al., 2013; Ude et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: After excluding all footprints encoding ProPro dipeptides, Pro still appeared to be slow at both positions 5 and 6.
source: We redid the original analysis after excluding all footprints encoding ProPro dipeptides. Results did not change significantly; Pro still appeared to be slow at both positions 5 and 6 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A.

claim: When looking specifically at footprints containing a ProPro dipeptide, there was a very large peak at position 5.
source: On the other hand, when we looked specifically at footprints containing a ProPro dipeptide, there was a very large peak at position 5 (Figure 6B), consistent with the very slow peptide bond formation seen in studies cited above.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: All five data sets gave qualitatively similar results for RRT analysis.
source: To establish repeatability, we generated and analyzed three other ribosome profiling datasets and also re-analyzed previously published data (Ingolia et al., 2009). All five data sets gave qualitatively similar results; pairwise correlations for RRTs at position 6 ranged from 0.22 to 0.96 between the datasets (Table 3).
evidence: This is shown in Table 3 with correlation values.

claim: The poorest correlation (0.22) was with the previously published dataset, which was generated using significantly different methods.
source: The poorest correlation (0.22) was a correlation with the previously published dataset, which was generated using significantly different methods than our datasets. In particular, that dataset was generated by adding cycloheximide to the growing culture, then harvesting (Ingolia et al., 2009), whereas our data were generated by flash-freezing first, then adding cycloheximide to the frozen cells.
evidence: This comparison is shown in Table 3 and explained by methodological differences.

claim: There are strong correlations between codon usage, the number of tRNA genes for the relevant tRNA, and tRNA abundance.
source: There are strong correlations between codon usage, the number of tRNA genes for the relevant tRNA, and tRNA abundance (Ikemura, 1981, 1982; Dong et al., 1996; Tuller et al., 2010; Novoa and Ribas de Pouplana, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from multiple cited studies.

claim: The correlation between codon usage and tRNA abundance is consistent with the idea that the rate of decoding in translation is at least partly limited by tRNA concentration.
source: Although one cannot determine causation from this correlation (Plotkin and Kudla, 2011), nevertheless it is consistent with the idea that the rate of decoding in translation is at least partly limited by tRNA concentration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed correlations.

claim: In yeast, the 61 sense codons are decoded by only 42 tRNAs.
source: In yeast, the 61 sense codons are decoded by only 42 tRNAs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the yeast tRNA complement.

claim: There are 12 pairs of codons that share a single tRNA in yeast.
source: There are 12 pairs of codons that share a single tRNA (e.g., Phe TTC and TTT; Tyr TAT and TAC; etc) (Roth, 2012).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about yeast tRNA-codon pairing.

claim: In many but not all cases, the RRT of two codons sharing the same tRNA is similar.
source: In many but not all cases, the RRT of the two codons is similar (Table 2), consistent with the 'concentration' hypothesis.
evidence: This observation is based on data in Table 2.

claim: There are cases where the RRT appears to be significantly different for two codons sharing the same tRNA.
source: However, there are also cases where the RRT appears to be significantly different for two codons sharing the same tRNA. For instance, the Cys codon TGC has an RRT of 1.23, while TGT has an RRT of 0.81 (Table 2). Both codons are recognized by the same tRNA, which in this case is complementary for TGC, and wobble for TGT.
evidence: This is shown in Table 2 with specific examples.

claim: The Gly codon GGC has an RRT of 1.22 (tRNA is complementary), while GGT has an RRT of 0.93 (tRNA is wobble).
source: Similarly, the Gly codon GGC has an RRT of 1.22 (tRNA is complementary), while GGT has an RRT of 0.93 (tRNA is wobble).
evidence: This is based on data in Table 2.

claim: Both the relationships RRT for TGC > TGT and RRT for GGC > GGT were true in all five datasets.
source: Both these relationships (RRT for TGC > TGT, and RRT for GGC > GGT) were true in all five datasets (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This consistency across datasets is noted.

claim: In both cases (TGC/TGT and GGC/GGT), the perfect match is decoded more slowly than the wobble match.
source: In both the cases, the perfect match is decoded more slowly than the wobble match and in both cases, the slower, complementary pairing has a G:C match at the third (i.e., wobble) position.
evidence: This pattern is observed in the data.

claim: The RRT depends on more than just the concentration of the relevant tRNA.
source: These and other similar examples (not shown) suggest that the RRT depends on more than just the concentration of the relevant tRNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that codons sharing the same tRNA can have different RRTs.

claim: The long RRTs for GC-rich codons might be related to the time needed to eject incorrectly paired anti-codons of incorrect tRNAs.
source: Perhaps the long RRTs for these GC-rich codons are related to the time needed to eject incorrectly paired anti-codons of incorrect tRNAs, although this explanation is somewhat at odds with the literature (Daviter et al., 2006; Gromadski et al., 2006).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about a possible mechanism.

claim: It has been suggested that translocation can occur more quickly when the codon:anticodon interaction is weaker.
source: Alternatively, it has been suggested that translocation can occur more quickly when the codon:anticodon interaction is weaker (Semenkov et al., 2000; Khade and Joseph, 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from cited literature.

claim: Lareau et al. discovered that ribosome profiling on cells not treated with any drug yields two classes of footprints: long (28–30 nucleotides) and short (20–22 nucleotides).
source: Recently, Lareau et al. made the exciting discovery that ribosome profiling on cells that have not been treated with any drug yields two classes of footprints, long (28–30 nucleotides) and short (20–22 nucleotides) (Lareau et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from the cited study by Lareau et al.

claim: The long class of footprints is seen in cycloheximide experiments.
source: It is the long class that is seen in cycloheximide experiments, and which we have characterized above.
evidence: This is stated based on the Lareau et al. findings.

claim: The short (20–22 nuc.) footprints seem to represent a different conformation of the ribosome, perhaps one that occurs when the ribosome translocates along the mRNA.
source: The short (20–22 nuc.) footprints seem to represent a different conformation of the ribosome, perhaps one that occurs when the ribosome translocates along the mRNA.
evidence: This is an interpretation from the Lareau et al. study.

claim: Treatment of cells with the elongation inhibitor anisomycin efficiently generates short footprints.
source: Furthermore, Lareau et al. found that treatment of cells with the elongation inhibitor anisomycin efficiently generates short footprints.
evidence: This is a finding from the cited Lareau et al. study.

claim: Lareau et al. suggest that the long and short footprints are reporting on two different states of translation.
source: Lareau et al. suggest that the long and short footprints are reporting on two different states of translation (Lareau et al., 2014).
evidence: This is the interpretation from the cited study.

claim: The pairwise correlations between the RRT results for the three anisomycin datasets from Lareau et al. were very high, ranging from 0.89 to 0.998.
source: We applied RRT analysis to the short footprints generated by Lareau et al., with special focus on the footprints after anisomycin treatment. All three of their anisomycin datasets were studied, and the pairwise correlations between the RRT results for these three datasets were very high, ranging from 0.89 to 0.998.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of Lareau et al. data.

claim: RRT values for the short footprints did not significantly correlate with RRT values for the long footprints, even when the phases of the footprints were shifted.
source: The RRT values for the short footprints did not significantly correlate with RRT values for the long footprints, even when the phases of the footprints were shifted.
evidence: This is a result from comparing the two types of footprint data.

claim: The lack of correlation between short and long footprint RRT values suggests that the short and long footprints are reporting on different translational processes.
source: This suggests, in agreement with Lareau et al., that the short and long footprints are indeed reporting on different translational processes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of correlation between the two datasets.

claim: For the short footprints, the RRT values are amino acid-specific, while for the long footprints at position 6, the RRT values are codon-specific.
source: Furthermore, for the short footprints the RRT values are amino acid-specific, while for the long footprints at position 6, the RRT values are codon-specific (Table 2; Table 4; Figure 4, Figure 7, Figure 8).
evidence: This is shown in the cited tables and figures.

claim: The difference between amino acid-specific and codon-specific effects indicates that the two kinds of footprints are reporting on different translational processes.
source: This again indicates that the two kinds of footprints are reporting on different translational processes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the different patterns observed.

claim: For short footprints, the peak at position 3 contains glycine.
source: The amino acids in the peaks at positions 3, 5, and 6 are shown in Table 4: the peak at position 3 contains glycine; the peak at position 5 contains smallish hydrophobic amino acids (Leu, Val, Ile, and to some extent Phe), and the peak at position 6 is dominated by the two basic amino acids, Arg and Lys.
evidence: This is shown in Table 4.

claim: For short footprints, the peak at position 5 contains smallish hydrophobic amino acids (Leu, Val, Ile, and to some extent Phe).
source: The amino acids in the peaks at positions 3, 5, and 6 are shown in Table 4: the peak at position 3 contains glycine; the peak at position 5 contains smallish hydrophobic amino acids (Leu, Val, Ile, and to some extent Phe), and the peak at position 6 is dominated by the two basic amino acids, Arg and Lys.
evidence: This is shown in Table 4.

claim: For short footprints, the peak at position 6 is dominated by the two basic amino acids, Arg and Lys.
source: The amino acids in the peaks at positions 3, 5, and 6 are shown in Table 4: the peak at position 3 contains glycine; the peak at position 5 contains smallish hydrophobic amino acids (Leu, Val, Ile, and to some extent Phe), and the peak at position 6 is dominated by the two basic amino acids, Arg and Lys.
evidence: This is shown in Table 4.

claim: It has been shown that basic amino acids can cause a pause in elongation by interacting with the ribosome exit tunnel.
source: It has previously been shown that basic amino acids can cause a pause in elongation by interacting with the ribosome exit tunnel (Lu et al., 2007; Lu and Deutsch, 2008; Brandman et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2012; Charneski and Hurst, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge from multiple cited studies.

claim: The application of RRT analysis to the anisomycin-generated footprints gives strong specific signals that are unlikely to be explained by a random process.
source: Nevertheless, the application of RRT analysis to the anisomycin-generated footprints gives strong specific signals that are unlikely to be explained by a random process.
evidence: This is an inference based on the strength and specificity of the observed signals.

claim: Results from the short footprints from untreated (no anisomycin) cells are only modestly correlated (0.23) with results from short footprints from the anisomycin-treated cells.
source: We note, however, that results from the short footprints from untreated (no anisomycin) cells are only modestly correlated (0.23) with results from short footprints from the anisomycin-treated cells (data not shown).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between two datasets.

claim: This is the first measurement of the differential rate of translation of all 61 codons in vivo.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first measurement of the differential rate of translation of all 61 codons in vivo.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: There is a correlation between a high codon usage and a high rate of decoding.
source: There is a correlation between a high codon usage and a high rate of decoding.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study supported by Figure 5A.

claim: Although the correlation between high codon usage and high decoding rate has been widely expected, there has been little evidence for it.
source: Although this is a correlation that has been widely expected, there has been little evidence for it; indeed, the most recent experiments suggested that all codons were decoded at the same rate (Qian et al., 2012; Charneski and Hurst, 2013).
evidence: This contextualizes the finding relative to previous work.

claim: An important theory was that the more common codons were common because their translation might be more accurate.
source: For instance, an important theory was that the more common codons were common because their translation might be more accurate (Plotkin and Kudla, 2011) (and this still might be correct).
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis from the cited literature.

claim: Translation is optimized for both speed and accuracy.
source: Translation is optimized for both speed and accuracy (Bieling et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited literature.

claim: During translation, the ribosome must sample many incorrect tRNAs at the A-site before finding a correct tRNA.
source: During translation, the ribosome must sample many incorrect tRNAs at the A-site before finding a correct tRNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the translation mechanism.

claim: After matching the anti-codon of the correct tRNA with the codon, there is a conformational change around the codon–anticodon interaction at the decoding center.
source: It must match the anti-codon of that correct tRNA with the codon; after such matching, there is a conformational change around the codon–anticodon interaction at the decoding center (Demeshkina et al., 2012; Zeng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited literature.

claim: The findings that (i) the more frequent codons are decoded rapidly; (ii) GC-rich codons are decoded slowly; and (iii) proline is slow in the P-site, suggest that there are at least three processes that happen somewhat slowly and on a similar timescale.
source: Our findings that (i) the more frequent codons (i.e., the ones with the highest tRNA concentrations) are decoded rapidly; and (ii) GC-rich codons are decoded slowly; and (iii) proline is slow in the P-site, suggest that there are at least three processes that happen somewhat slowly and on a similar timescale.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The high rate of decoding for high concentration tRNAs may reflect the relatively short time it takes for the ribosome to find a high-concentration correct tRNA among many incorrect tRNAs.
source: The high rate of decoding for high concentration tRNAs may reflect the relatively short time it takes for the ribosome to find a high-concentration correct tRNA among many incorrect tRNAs.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the findings.

claim: The fact that proline-specific delays are of similar magnitude to rare-codon specific delays suggests that peptide bond formation and identification of the correct tRNA are happening on similar time scales.
source: The fact that we detect proline-specific delays of a similar magnitude to the rare-codon specific delays suggest that peptide bond formation and identification of the correct tRNA are happening on similar time scales.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of delay magnitudes.

claim: If one process was entirely rate-limiting in protein synthesis, there would be very strong selection for greater speed in that process, until it 'catches up' with other processes.
source: In general, this is what one might expect from the evolution of such an important process as protein synthesis—if one process was entirely rate-limiting, there would be very strong selection for greater speed in that process, until a point is reached where it 'catches up' with other processes, and several processes together are then rate-limiting.
evidence: This is an evolutionary argument based on inference.

claim: The data establish that common codons are translated relatively rapidly, but this does not on its own explain the success of codon optimization for increasing protein expression, since the rate of translation is primarily limited by the rate of initiation, not elongation.
source: Even though these data establish that common codons are translated relatively rapidly, this does not on its own explain the success of codon optimization for increasing protein expression, since the rate of translation is primarily limited by the rate of initiation, not elongation (Andersson and Kurland, 1990; Plotkin and Kudla, 2011) (although one recent study identifies a mechanism whereby rapid elongation causes rapid initiation [Chu et al., 2014]).
evidence: This is a discussion of the implications of the findings in light of cited literature.

claim: On a genome-wide scale, the use of faster codons would mean that a given genomic set of mRNAs would require fewer ribosomes to make a given amount of protein than the same set of mRNAs using slower codons.
source: Nevertheless, on a genome-wide (and not gene-specific) scale, the use of faster codons would mean that a given genomic set of mRNAs would require (or titrate out) fewer ribosomes to make a given amount of protein than the same set of mRNAs using slower codons (Andersson and Kurland, 1990; Plotkin and Kudla, 2011).
evidence: This is an inference about the genome-wide implications of the findings, supported by citations.

claim: Based on RRT measurements and taking into account different copy numbers of different mRNAs, yeast requires about 5% fewer ribosomes than if they were to make protein at the same overall rate but using each synonymous codon at an equal frequency.
source: Based on our RRT measurements, and taking into account the different copy numbers of different mRNAs (Lipson et al., 2009), we roughly estimate that yeast requires about 5% fewer ribosomes than if they were to make protein at the same overall rate but using each synonymous codon at an equal frequency ('Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a quantitative estimate based on the RRT data and mRNA abundance data.

claim: The 5% reduction in ribosome requirement provides at least a sufficient reason for the bias towards faster synonymous codons.
source: This provides at least a sufficient reason for the bias towards faster synonymous codons.
evidence: This is an inference about the evolutionary significance of the findings.

claim: One speculative possibility is that the short footprint results report on the interaction of amino acids in the nascent peptide chain with the exit tunnel of the ribosome.
source: While we know too little about the nature of the short footprints to reliably interpret these results, one speculative possibility is that the results report on the interaction of amino acids in the nascent peptide chain with the exit tunnel of the ribosome (Raue et al., 2007; Petrone et al., 2008; Berndt et al., 2009; Bhushan et al., 2010; Lu et al., 2011; Wilson and Beckmann, 2011; Gumbart et al., 2012).

claim: The finding that Arg and Lys are slow at position 6 in short footprints correlates with the fact that these basic amino acids cause a pause by interacting with the exit tunnel.
source: We find Arg and Lys slow at position 6, and this correlates with the fact that these basic amino acids cause a pause by interacting with the exit tunnel (Lu et al., 2007; Lu and Deutsch, 2008; Brandman et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2012; Charneski and Hurst, 2013).

claim: The pattern in short footprints suggests that small hydrophobic amino acids, and then glycine, might cause pauses by interacting with positions one or three amino acids further out in the exit tunnel.
source: This would then suggest that small hydrophobic amino acids, and then glycine, might similarly cause pauses by interacting with positions one or three amino acids further out in the exit tunnel.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed pattern.

source: In summary, we believe that RRT analysis is a sensitive high-resolution method that can characterize the interaction of codons and amino acids with the ribosome.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of the method based on the results obtained.
